utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, I'm Tom Hannis, with Belinda Pidwell, and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for the Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic appearing for Zupljanin Defence this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And could the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Bajagic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, before Mr. Zecevic resumes, I remind you of the solemn declaration that you made yesterday. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we broke off when you were commenting upon footnote 13, 1D78. When I asked you yesterday, I think I gave you the wrong reference. Well, relatively speaking. Because in that part of your report, you also mention this in 169 and 170, but basically you deal with this document in paragraphs 123 and 124, on page 43 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, for the record, the page references between the Serbian and the English aren't the same, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh I'm really sorry. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The paragraphs are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The paragraphs are. Okay. Thank you very much. Sorry, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have a look at your footnote 148. That is in paragraph 124. This is tab 33. 396 -- 65 ter 3961.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. This is a particular footnote and document of which we have an objection. It's refers to the testimony of Mr. Delimustafic in a trial in State Court. We think the -- if there's any effort to have this exhibit tendered through this witness, it should be denied. It's -- attempting to introduce it through this witness is trying to get around the provisions of Rule 92. If they want the evidence of Mr. Delimustafic, he could be called as a Defence witness. It's not appropriate to try and introduce his testimony in another Tribunal in this fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, let me hear from Mr. Zecevic, but I confess that the impression I had is that this was by way of reference and you are anticipating at this point. But you may be correct. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I anticipated that this was going to be the objection, and I didn't want to tender the witness -- the document as an exhibit. But since the -- since the expert refers to it in his footnotes, I -- I need to -- I need to get the explanation from him why and for what purpose and I believe I'm entitled to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, am I missing something? Having regard to the limited purpose for which, if I understand Mr. Zecevic correctly, he is asking the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess I need to hear the questions and the answer and then make a submission at that time. What I'm trying to avoid is getting in the content of that evidence in this fashion because I see it as a way to try and avoid the requirements of Rule 92 ter. But let's hear what follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, your footnote 148, paragraph 124 of your report, you refer to this document that is a transcript of the testimony of Mr. Alija Delimustafic in the case of Momcilo Mandic. Could you tell us why, what the reason was, for you to cite this document in your paper? Why are you referring to this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I guess what I would request is before that question is answered, that Your Honours are directed to the paragraph or the sentences to which this footnote is supposed to be support for so that you can understand why it's being offered. At page 50 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, at the very beginning, I said we stopped at the footnote 13 and that is the -- the 1st of April collegium meeting of MUP SRBiH, and that is the reference on the document which is -- which is the focus of -- of paragraphs 123 and 124 of the expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Page 50, paragraph 124, immediately after footnote 147 in the text the sentence begins: "It is evident from the instruction that the result of the collegium was the factual recognition of the existence of a MUP of the Serbian People of BH which is additionally confirmed by the fact that the minutes from the collegium were also sent to the ministers of the interior, 'Mico Stanisic and Alija Delimustafic' as well as the SSUP (Federal Secretariat of the Interior) and others." Footnote 148; that's what it's supposed to support.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is -- I mean, Mr. Hannis will have the opportunity to cross-examine the expert witness. The expert witness made the reference to this document in his -- in his expert report. I'm just trying to find out what is the reason, and I am inviting the expert, the author, to explain this to us. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bajagic, I have put a question to you. If you still remember it, please answer.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I remember. This footnote has to do only with the last part of this paragraph, or, rather, the last sentence. In order to support the comment that the result of that collegium was accepting the fact that the MUP of the Serbian Republic of BH did exist, and the gentleman did state --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, which gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Alija Delimustafic, who was minister of the interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He confirmed that the transcript of that collegium was sent to the ministers of the interior, Mico Stanisic of the Serb Republic of BH, to him, and Mr. Delimustafic as well as to the Federal Secretariat of The interior, in Belgrade that is. And to other organs. So the reason why I refer to this document, is because Mr. Alija Delimustafic confirmed the fact that he knew everything about the collegium that had been held, that he knew what the results were because he personally received the minutes of collegium meeting. Nothing else is relevant here except for that fact, and that is why it was included.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bajagic, paragraph 127, we've already mentioned it. We mentioned it yesterday. It refers to the legal framework, if I can put it that way, for the functioning of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serb Republic in the period from April to December, and the sources are provided here. I would like to ask you to give us brief comments. I know that you're not a lawyer by training, but could you just give us brief comments with regard to these legal regulations that are mentioned here in your paper. I see that under the fourth bullet point, after the constitution and the amendments to the constitution, the Law on the Government is referred to. Can you explain to us why you put it there and why it is important for understanding the legal framework within which the MUP of the Serb Republic functioned in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Law on the Government is the topmost law, after the constitution, that regulates the functioning of the government and the ministries, and as we can see on the basis of this expert report, there are two paragraphs concerning this law. 133 and 134. Two particular articles of that law are referred to: That is Article 6 in which it says that among the other members of the government, that is to say, the government and the members of the government, it is the minister of the interior who is also appointed. The other important article is Article 19 that refers to the duties of the members of the government. And, finally, Article 13 states the rights and responsibilities of the members of the government to put on the agenda of government meetings various important issues and so on and so forth. So whatever pertains to other ministers pertains to the minister of the interior as well. And that is why this reference was made to the Law on the Government, which is one of the system-based laws, and it has to do with the functioning of the Ministry of the Interior as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. By way of a reference, this is tab 30, your footnote 142.1, P734. The next regulation that you refer to in paragraphs 135 and 136 is the Law on State Administration. That is tab 37; your footnote 156. And it is part of law library here; L32 is the reference. Could you please give us your comment? Could you tell us why this law is important for your research?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Law on State Administration is of exceptional importance for the organisation and functioning of the Ministry of the Interior and also for the position of the minister of the interior, who is an elected official in charge of that organ. As we can see in paragraph 135, what is particularly highlighted are Articles 11 and 12 of this law, referring to the rights and responsibilities of executive organs and administrative organs in the discharge of the functioning of the state administration. These articles and this law show that the Ministry of the Interior within the system of the executive government is one of the administration's agencies because in Article 19 of the Law on Administration, it says that administrative organs in the given system are organised as ministries, secretariats, and administrations. At the level of the republic, it is ministries and republican administration; and at lower levels, the level of lower social communities, it is secretariats and administrations. So what follows is that the Ministry of the Interior is a state organ at the level of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bajagic. Could you please give us a brief comment. Further on in your expert report you touched upon this issue. However, since we are now dealing with this particular piece of legislation, I would like us to discuss it now. It has to do with Articles 38 and 39, and it is within the chapter on state organs and how they are run.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, since state organs at the republican level are called ministers and secretariats, Article 38 of this law states that the minister is in charge of the ministry, and a secretariat -- a secretary is in charge of a secretariat. In Article 39, things are spelled out in greater detail. Namely, what the duties are of the official who was in charge of a particular state organ. In view of this law, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say an official who is in charge, does that mean the minister or the secretary, or someone else?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers to the official that is in charge of the organ and represents it. So it is the minister, if we're talking about a ministry; and it's the secretary, if we're talking about a secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next piece of legislation that you refer to, Mr. Bajagic, in paragraph 137 of your expert report is the Law on Ministries. By way of reference, it is tab 31; your footnote 142.2. It is part of the law library; L34 is the number. Could you please give us your brief comment.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case as well, it is a system-related law of exceptional importance for each and every organ of the state administration that is at ministry rank. Therefore, the Ministry of the Interior included. In general terms, this law spells out in more specific terms what the fields of work are of all the ministries that are established on the basis of this law. Namely, in Article 1 of this law, it says that: "This law shall establish ministries as republican government organs and republican government organisations and establish their competencies," their province of work. In this connection, it is very important to look at both Articles 1 and 8 of the Law on Ministries, and that Article specifically deals with the position of the Ministry of the Interior in the system of ministries that exists. According to that Article, it is stated unequivocally that the Ministry of the Interior carries out administrative and other professional work related to an entire set of issues that have to do with the overall mission and vision of the Ministry of the Interior. That is the significance of these two Articles related to ministries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, could I just put a question to you that relates to Article 6 of the law. If the usher could get us back to the first page. Thank you. My question is to the order in which the ministries are lined up in Article 6. You see that the ministries shall be, first, the ministry of National Defence; secondly, the Ministry of the Interior; thirdly, the Ministry of Justice; then comes foreign affairs, finance, and so on, and so on. My question is: If, in this Article, there is a priority of importance in the way the ministries are listed, or do they just come by alphabetical order or by some other order that has nothing to do with the importance and the significance and the position within the government of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion, it's a list of 13 ministries, stating the ministries that are hereby established. There is no specific significance to the way they are lined up, because all the ministries are -- that are part of the executive branch of government of equal ranking and importance. If I had the possibility to draft a bill now, I would possibly place the Ministry for Information and Technological Development first. But in my view this is a list of no particular order and I don't believe that the ministry's placement on this list in any way reflects its significance in the government. They were all of equal importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, professor. Back to you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bajagic, through my fault, we omitted to mention something. But before we move onto the Law on the Ministry of the Interior, when I asked you about the Law on Government in paragraph 134 and footnote 155, and that's a document behind tab 36 here, and it is part of the law library, under L88, we see that the Law on Government of Republika Srpska was amended in September of 1992, as compared to the March 1992 version that we commented on. Can you give us your brief comment on this particular law, since we had two laws on the government in the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a law which was improved on the 15th of December, 1992. The amendment had to do with the substance and the way it was dealt with in the various articles. But no substantial issues were dealt with. Instead of Article such and such, it's a different Article that deals with a particular matter. So there is nothing else that could be raised in this other law and which would specifically have to do with the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraphs 138 and 139 and onwards, you speak of the system-related law; namely, the Law on the Interior --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is tab 32, your footnote 142.3. The document has been admitted as P530. As I said, you addressed this issue in paragraphs 138, 139, and onwards. Can we have your comment on the Law on the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Law on the Internal Affairs is one of the system-related laws and the topmost law dealing with all the matters pertaining to internal or home affairs, as such. Right at the beginning of the law, the province of internal affairs is set out specifically - that's in Article 3 of the law - which says that the province of the home affairs will cover the affairs of public and state security, tasks and affairs of national security, and tasks and affairs pertaining to a number of administration-related issues, from the issuance of identity papers to a number of others. Article 4 states that internal affairs are affairs of general interest to the republic itself. As can be clearly seen from these various articles, which deal with matters ranging from generic to specific as we will see later on ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For the information of counsel, the Court Officer just confirmed something to me. I was curious why this was a Prosecution exhibit rather than part of the law library. But I am reminded that this was exhibited before we come up with the concept of the law library.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead, Mr. Bajagic. Continue with your answer. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, as we will see in our subsequent analysis, the law deals with the entire province of internal affairs from generic to specific issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, tell us very briefly, in connection with paragraph 139, where you explain the substance of the law, what was the basic division in structural terms within the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the law in its entirety, the global structure of the ministry was set out in such a way that it was constituted of two global units; one was the Public Security Service, and the other National Security Service. The law provides that, in addition to the minister's office, the other two are topmost leaders. Within the ministry would be the individuals in charge of these two units. That's to say, the under-secretary for public security, and under-secretary for national security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown, unless there are objections from the Prosecution since I failed to announce this document, but my colleague, Mr. Hannis, did. Can the witness be shown P876, in order to give us his comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The usher will hand you my copy because it is a better copy. Mr. Bajagic, this folder is similar to the one that you looked at yesterday which had to do with the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The chart was made by the Prosecution for the purposes of their case. Please have a look at it and tell us if there's anything in particular you'd like to comment on with respect to the structure as presented in the chart.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the structure that we can see in the chart and in view of what I said, that there were two global units, we can see that we have the minister's office here, and below the two units, namely, on the left-hand side, the Public Security Service, and on the right-hand side, the National Security Service. As far as the factual situation is concerned, I believe that is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does the Law on the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina provide for the post of assistant to the minister?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, will you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I mean under the Law on the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the post of Assistant Minister? No, not under that piece of legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have a document in English here, and beneath Mr. Mico Stanisic's photograph, we have the name of Momcilo Mandic and his duty of Assistant Minister.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. But this wasn't what I was referring to when I was making my initial comments. It had to do with the two units. The law clearly states that in addition to the minister, the two top leadership positions are those of the under-secretary of public security and the under-secretary of national security, and the law is silent on anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. May I intervene just to raise a question. What we have on the screen lists Momcilo Mandic as deputy minister is the English explanation we have on the chart. It has been translated now as assistant minister. If we can have some clarification as to whether those two terms are equal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I haven't seen the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bajagic, can you give us a clear answer to have it interpreted well. Under the Law on the Home Affairs -- a moment, please. Under the Law on the Home Affairs of Republika Srpska from 1992 which is the subject of your research here, was the post of assistant minister envisaged or any other such post as would fit within the structure between the under-secretary -- under-secretaries of public and state security and the minister himself?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was quite clear a moment ago. In the structure between the post of minister and those of under-secretaries, there are no significant posts. The two functionaries are responsible to the minister for their respective provinces of work and in between there are no posts envisaged and the law is quite explicit on this. There is no function of assistant or deputy minister under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, again, Mr. Zecevic's question got translated as assistant. I understand we're talking about a person between the minister and the two under-secretaries. But my confusion is because at the next level when we have the heads of administration, they're all described as assistant ministers. Is there not a word in Serbian for "deputy" that is different than the word in Serbian for "assistant"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, there are two words. There is pomocnik, there is zamenik [Interpretation] And that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Pomocnik, assistant; zamenik, deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify matters. You have the document before you. As part of public security, there is a number of administrations. Can you list the administrations that fall within public security? And let us try and identify them on the chart that we have before us.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would make it easier for me if I referred to the law as well. But I do know that there is the administration for uniformed police, administration for the prevention and suppression of crime. At all times, there was an administration for communication and information, administration for training, personnel administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, look at the legal provisions and disregard the chart. What we want to establish is whether the chart reflects the law, and, of course, you will agree with me that it is the law that is the authoritative text, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the law is the authority. But, please, can you refer me to the paragraph where I listed it or to the relevant provisions of the law, rather than me flipping through the entire text of the law, and in that event I will be able to analyse the chart in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Give me a moment, please. Very well. Let's simplify the matter. Mr. Bajagic, the individuals heading a given administration within public security, what is their title? And I mean in the head office of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These individuals in charge of administrations are referred to at times as chiefs of administrations, and they may, at the same time, perform the duty of assistant ministers. It is not an ex officio position but they may at the same time be heads of administrations and assistant ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, if they are called assistant ministers, does that mean that they were still subordinated to the under-secretary for public or state security respectively?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All assistant ministers who are, at the same time, at the head of these organisational units in the public security department, are directly subordinated to the under-secretary for public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now take another look at the chart and the last comment from you. To the far right, you will see a line that links Mr. Mico Stanisic, or, rather, his photograph with a box in which it says "Sokolac, special police platoon, Commander Dusko Malovic." Can you comment on this, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see from the law itself, within the public security department and its administration for uniformed police, also operational was a special police brigade, and I know that that was stipulated by the law and that existed before in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Under the law, this special police brigade existed and this continued to exist in the MUP of Republika Srpska. It was part of the police administration and it was within the public security department. I can see that underneath here that there is mention of the special police brigade, although this is the first time that I'm seeing this kind of chart, which surprises me to see these functional links with the office of the minister of another unit. That would be my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Bajagic, the authority which Mr. Dusko Malovic is supposed to have under this chart, or in this chart - sorry - is that he is in charge of the Sokolac SJB, special police platoon. But there were special police units in other districts, weren't there? So my question is: Was Mr. Malovic only in charge of the special police in Sokolac, or was he also in charge of special police units in other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I honestly don't know. And I actually never addressed these issues in my expert analysis. I did not analyse any specific unit in the whole territory of the Serbian Republic of BH with the exception of one or maybe more paragraphs where I tackled the issue of a special police unit that operated in the Autonomous Region of Krajina. I addressed the fact that this unit had been disbanded and then a special police brigade was established in a centralised way in accordance with the law. That's why I said that I find it surprising to see these links. The fact is, if we accept this as a fact, it could indicate that maybe we could put another 30 boxes of the same kind relating to various regions. But I know that the special police brigade in the first year was part of the uniformed police department within the public security department. Under the law, during that period, no special police unit had any direct links with the office of the minister. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So why was Sokolac so special? Or perhaps the better question is: Was Sokolac, indeed, having or enjoying any special or particular position at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, and I learned these facts from the documents, the ministry head office or any other significant organisational unit was based in that town. When I analysed the documents that spoke about some combat operations, I realized that there were not even any direct combat operations conducted in or around Sokolac. Of course, I know where Sokolac is, and I'm familiar with that area, so in terms of discharging any crucial police work on even in military terms, it did not have any strategic significance higher than any other place. Quite the contrary. It was a town which was more peaceful than many other towns. So in that context, at least as far as the documents that I analysed are concerned, Sokolac does not feature as any special town. That is why I said that I was surprised to see this mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And then a follow-up question, perhaps, Professor. Who was the commander of the centralised special police unit, or brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of BH, once it was established according to the law, the commander of the special police brigade was Milenko Karisik. And I think I have mentioned that fact somewhere in my expert report. And, sorry, I'd like to say that this is this specific box that you can see here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... thank you. That's why I asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bajagic, before we analyse in more detail some other aspects of the Law on Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska as a systemic law, would you be so kind as to look at your footnote 178.1 which relates to your paragraph 145. That's tab 39. And in this case, just like the previous ones, it's marked as P510. That's the Law on Internal Affairs of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1990. Could you please just comment on the differences between this Law on Internal Affairs of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1990, and the Law on Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska from 1992.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I make comparison between specific provisions and paragraphs in these two laws, i.e., the BH law from 1990 and the Law on Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would like to underline that organisational units of the ministry according to territorial principle had certain obligations towards municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I just took this as a reference, this particular paragraph, not because of its contents but because of the fact that you established a link. My question was: If we compare the contents of the law of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Law on Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska, to what extent do these two laws differ and what is the essence of these differences?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two laws are identical for the greatest part. The majority of the provisions that govern the organisation, the functioning, the territorial organisation of the ministry are identical. There are, though, certain differences in a number of chapters, but I can't tell you that off the top of my head. Generally speaking, these two laws are similar, of course, and they regulate matters in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to the Law on Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska. A while ago, when we commented the chart, you explained to us that there were two main departments, the public security department and the state security department, that were headed by under-secretaries. Can you please explain to us what was the function of these under-secretaries with regard to the ministry and the administrations subordinated to them, and then what was the relationship between these under-secretaries and the minister of the interior? Under the law.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The under-secretaries for public and national security report to the minister of the interior, and those directly responsible to these two are, for example, in case of public security, is the chief of the administration for suppression and prevention of crime, which means all the heads of the sectors who are within the public security department are directly responsible to the under-secretary for public security. The same applies to the other department. When we talk about the under-secretary for national security, head of certain administrations that are part of this department are responsible to the under-secretary; whereas, the under-secretary himself is responsible to the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are the under-secretaries answerable to the minister of the interior, in terms of how their respective departments operate, or are they responsible for some other things?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law is very clear on that. They are answerable to the interior minister for the entire operation of the department that they are the head of, which means all important issues, starting from the organisation of the work that they are performing. In other words, the entire operation of the department, it is the under-secretary who reports to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, speaking about general issues pertaining to the functioning of the Ministry of the Interior, I would like to show you a number of documents that would serve as an illustration of what a ministry of the interior is practically involved in, and I would like to hear your comments on that. That's tab 1. The document is 65 ter 336D1. That's a Defence document. It's tab number 1. Sir, this is a document that has three pages. The first page is a report on an on-site investigation compiled, as we can see, on page 2, an investigating judge who signed it, and then page 3 is a record of external examination of the body. Can you briefly comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the legal regulations in force at the time and when the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina functioned and also at the time when the ministry of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina functioned, the Ministry of the Interior, and let me just specify a particular department. The public security department is responsible for safe-guarding the property of citizens, public law and order, and preventing and curbing all forms of crime. In the field of prevention and crime control, members of the Ministry of the Interior, or the relevant department within it, have certain duties in terms of carrying out certain activities with the representatives of other state organs and in respect of the commission of various crimes. So according to the system that was in force then, the Ministry of the Interior was duty-bound to send its authorised officers whose field of activity is crime control anyway, that is to say, crime inspectors, and also representatives of that those departments that deal with technical matters, right? The person in charge of the on-site investigation was the investigative judge in that system, and, of course, at the request of the investigating judge, the team on the scene can include other persons as well, in order to carry out a proper on-site investigation, in order to preserve material evidence that might indicate who the perpetrator of the crime was. From that point of view, this document precisely indicates that. We see who the persons present on the scene are. It's the Duty Judge, then the representatives of the military post, the forensic medicine doctor. That is what I can say about this record. Because I don't really know anything else about medicine. And I don't see anything controversial here. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could I just ask you to give us an explanation. You said in your response that the Ministry of the Interior has the duty to send its authorised officers, a crime inspector, and an inspector from the department that includes crime technicians, the forensic departments. Could you tell us what these inspectors, these forensic inspectors do, the crime technicians?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, these inspectors, crime technicians, take part in securing the scene of the crime; then also keeping the traces there; taking various objects in accordance with the rules involved. So these measures are taken, these technical measures, and all of them with a view to preserving material evidence in the best possible way, the evidence that might indicate who the perpetrator was and that is important for the process that is to ensue. That is what crime technicians do, these inspectors. There are many forensic matters involved, but what is done on the scene itself involves this kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not sure for what purpose or how it relates to any contested matter in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by way of illustration. I think it's a relevant document. Because it is a record of an on-site investigation during the relevant period of time, the time relevant to this indictment. It has to do with a crime that occurred in a municipality that is included in the indictment and where the victim was a person who was an ethnic Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For myself, Mr. Zecevic, the -- in terms of public security matters this is almost routine. What -- I appreciate you're saying it's illustrative, but it isn't remarkable in any way, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, it is not at all remarkable. I just wanted to -- I'm leading another questions and you will see where I'm going with this line. I'm not insisting on admitting this document. I'm just -- I thought just as illustration of the -- of the -- of the expert opinion given on -- during his testimony. And there are some additional reasons why this document, in my opinion, is relevant, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, could I hear those other reasons and respond to them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I just stated them. It's a crime that happened in the relevant time in one of the municipalities which is in the indictment and the victim is a lady of the Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I guess if it is to rebut the Prosecution's position that the police weren't investigating or prosecuting crimes where the suspected perpetrators were Serbs and the victims were non-Serbs, it may have some relevance. However, I think this only indicates that an on-site investigation was done, which would be the judge doing something. There's no evidence that the police then followed -- followed up and filed a criminal report. And the absence of that is consistent with our theory, that the police were not pursuing these matters. I think we have had witnesses from Kljuc talking about what is in the KU reports, and I don't believe this one is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zecevic, the victim of this crime is not in the victims' list in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not entirely sure, Your Honours, but I can give you an answer after the break. Because the -- the surname does sound a bell. But it might be -- it might be the case that, that it has been mentioned during the case in some other -- in other relation. Maybe we can take the break now and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, while the witness is on his way in, we have been alerted by the Court Officer that the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yeah, I know. Has requested ten minutes at the end of the day, so you will pace yourself accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was notified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you abandoned your application to have this document admitted, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We checked, and it is not in the schedules. The name of the victim is not in the schedules, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, tell me, please, from a technical point of view, if I can put it that way, in the so-called pre-criminal proceedings, where does the role of the police end?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role of the Ministry of the Interior and its members ends when the criminal report is filed, regardless of whether the perpetrator is known or unknown. That is how far police powers go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tab 3. 340D1 is the 65 ter number. This is a document dated the 2nd of December, 1992. It is a criminal report. It's actually a set of documents. Five or six documents are attached. Could you please give us your brief comment on this document.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document -- or, rather, this criminal report, confirms my previous statement. We see that it is the public security station of Kotor Varos that filed this criminal report. It was the head of the public security station that filed this criminal report. We see that there's a reference to the relevant laws on the basis of which it is being filed, and we see that the general pattern is followed there against whom it is being filed - in this case, the perpetrator is unknown - and then various facts are given about the said person. Then there's a description of the crime. And then the evidence that is just listed briefly. And then there are the attachments that are enclosed. So they're an integral part of the criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What are the usual attachments that are enclosed with a criminal report? Could you please tell us that.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is certainly a record of the on-site investigation that is written up by the investigative judge. Then if there was expertise carried out by doctors, then there are documents about that. And then there is an Official Note of the members of the Ministry of the Interior who wrote that. And it has to do with a specific crime, when information was being collected about material evidence and about the perpetrator of the crime involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "expertise of a doctor," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that can be a record or a certificate of death, if the injured party died; and it can also be a medical certificate, if there were grave injuries sustained, or other things that belonged to the domain of medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is a traffic incident, then it could also include some expertise by a traffic expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, bearing in mind Mr. Hannis's objection from a while ago, I think that this document meets all the requirements, as it were, that Mr. Hannis referred to in relation to the previous document we tendered, so I would like to tender this document as relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, are you able to indicate the ethnicity of the victim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the description of the crime, there is only a reference to the name, or, rather, the last name, and I don't see any reference to ethnicity. Baric; that is what is written here. I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think there is an indication of his first name also, Jako. So the name Jako Baric does not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jako Baric, yes. But I cannot say what that person's ethnicity was, only on the basis of the name and surname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, what has this document have that the previous one doesn't have?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, Mr. Hannis objected to the previous document, saying that the position of the Office of the Prosecutor is not that -- that the -- that the Ministry of the Interior was not conducting on-site investigations. The point they are -- they -- they are pursuing is that the ministry was conducting on-site investigations but was not filing criminal complaints against the perpetrator where the victim is a non-Serb. Now I cannot say for sure that this person is -- is not non-Serb, but it -- it sounds very much like a Croat name and surname. But I wouldn't like to give evidence on this. But it's -- it's the -- it's the -- it's the matter of doubt that I think we are in entitled to have in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But is it related to the facts and the crimes we're dealing with here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I mean, if it's a -- a, for instance, a crime of passion, and even if it's somebody of Croatian or -- or Muslim ethnicity who is concerned, is that relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... the fact that investigations are conducted in those cases relevant to this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, according to this criminal complaint, it says that on the 2nd of November, 1992, around 8.00, two unknown men dressed -- between 20 and 30, dressed in olive-drab uniforms, armed with automatic rifles, shot at the -- at the windows of the house, and committed a murder of this person. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. I must admit that I missed that. I was checking the victims' list. He's not on the victim's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's not on the victim list, but Kotor Varos municipality is in the -- in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D532, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another document, Mr. Bajagic, behind tab 4. It's 65 ter 374D1. It's an entire criminal case file of which the military court in Bijeljina was seized. Let's go through the documents that make up this file, and can we have your brief comments on them.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Pause there. Before you start giving your answer, let me state for Their Honours that it's a document dated the 27th of September, 1992. The crime scene is in Bijeljina municipality, which is referred in our indictment, and it is the murder of one Enes Tabakovic who is apparently a Muslim, because, on page 2, it says that the person murdered had been taken prisoner in August 1992 and was held within the barracks in Bijeljina. Can we have your comments now.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a set of documents. First of all, a record of the on-site investigation was made on the part of military investigation bodies. We can see that the investigative judge is Captain Radusa Bojcic. We have the forensic technician and note-taker, all of whom are members of the army, in contrast to the previous document where we had a civilian investigative judge, a member of the Ministry of the Interior, and a number of other individuals. The record of the on-site investigation describes the crime committed. We also have an Official Note here, which was compiled by the authorised official of the military police, I presume. We also have the criminal report filed by Commander Captain First Class Dragomir Keserovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's page 7 in e-court in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was filed by a military prosecutor attached to a certain military post. And, lastly, we have the judgement rendered by the court seized of the criminal report and all the other documentation. Finally, the same set of documents contains a judgement rendered by the Supreme Court of Republika Srpska, denying the appeal lodged by the defendants in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, in your view, is this case illustrative of the way in which a criminal procedure unfolded under the regulation in force at the time -- under the regulations in force at the time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see that there are two procedures here. The civilian procedure, and a procedure which took place under a set of military regulations. In technical terms, the procedures are probably similar, but in view of the bodies involved, from prosecutor's offices to investigative judges, to judges, are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, in the civilian criminal procedure, does the procedure initiate with the criminal report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The criminal report is the basis from which everything else follows. I don't know much about it because I am not an expert in the area, but I do know up until what point the police are involved, and I do know that there was the system of the military judiciary from the prosecutor's offices to the judges of the courts of both instances performing their respective duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The civilian criminal procedure, as far as you know, did it end with a judgement?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the customary practice across the world. Every criminal procedure ends with a judgement. There may be other specifics involved that I cannot go into right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document into evidence. I think that it is useful as an illustration and relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the relevance is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I suppose by way of illustration, it's the -- it's a specimen of a complete case from start to finish. And this is one of the -- and bearing in mind that this witness is an expert, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D533.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With your last comment in mind, Your Honour, I just want to state on the record that it's our position that he's tendered as a police expert. He, himself, just said now that he is not an expert on criminal procedure in terms of in terms of military or civilian courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We haven't forgotten the Prosecution's position on that, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, we will now go back to the Law on the Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska behind tab 32. Your footnote 142.3; Exhibit P530. In paragraphs 148, where you explain Article 33, and the following paragraphs, in paragraph 148, you list the various powers of the Ministry of the Interior under Article 33. Let us start with Article -- or, rather, paragraph 149, and could you please give us your brief comments on each and every competence or power as envisaged under the law.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the fact that the province of the internal affairs comprises public security, national security, and a number of affairs relating to administration --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have Article 33 in e-court. It's page 4 in the Serbian and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 33 of the Law on Internal Affairs sets out the service of national security and regulates that the MUP shall discharge, perform duties of national security. And that's in the first bullet point: "Directly conduct national security-related activities ..." We have already referred to this one of the two global units within the MUP; namely, the National Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am referring to Article 33 of the Law on Internal Affairs, which reads -- yeah, I'm sorry. You were referring to the first answer --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the first bullet point of the various bullet points listing the duties and tasks of the ministry as a whole, which deals with national security as the first set of tasks within that ministry. And I was just going back to what I said earlier on, that this was one of the two units within the ministry which has its own respective organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the National Security Service, subsequently the law would define the internal structure of the service as regulated -- or to be regulated subsequently in a set of regulations or rules which are actually bylaws. So that's one of the various competencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please go through all the competences under Article 33 that are mentioned in the subsequent paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministry at its seat shall, furthermore, monitor, direct, and coordinate the activity of the Security Services Centre and public security stations, especially in activities related to public security. In cases of higher complexity, if necessary, it shall take direct measures to prevent and detect crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Next.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next is the protection of citizens and their personal security and lives, as well as the protection of facilities and other material goods. In cases of general emergency or serious breaches of public law and order. Next is the competence whereby the Ministry of the Interior shall, at its seat, monitor the administration of internal affairs entrusted to other organs, enterprises and legal entities. Moreover, the ministry shall, at its seat, prepare or draft the proposal for the organisation and the strength of the reserve police force in the republic, as well as the criteria for its manning, or the recruitment of its personnel. In this respect, the ministry has the power to activate the reserve police force in emergency situations upon orders from the president of the republic, as defined by other system-related laws and the constitution itself. Likewise, the ministry shall, at its headquarters, see to it that weapons are procured, as well as other appropriate sets of equipment for the needs of the active duty and reserve force from the funds earmarked for those purposes in the republican budget. Furthermore, the ministry has the power to set up professional and specialised training programmes for the active-duty and reserve police forces and other authorised officials and test -- or, rather, deal with other forms of training and exercise. Furthermore, the ministry is under the obligation to advance the specialist and scientific methods of work, as well as the subject matter of the work of the Public Security Service. Its next competence has to do with the organisation development, modernisation, and maintenance of communication systems of the Ministry of the Interior, as well as their protection overall. The next competence of the ministry headquarters is to perform complex forensic analysis for the needs of Security Services Centres and public security stations. The ministry headquarters is also authorised to ensure the introduction and application of modern scientific methods in crime prevention. It is also in charge of cooperating with foreign organs and international organisations in the field of internal affairs. Its next competence is to issue local search notices and publish appropriate bulletins on searches. And, finally, the ministry headquarters is in charge, or competent, to keep mandatory and other necessary records of statistical and operational data and ensure that such records are kept in all Security Services Centres and public security stations. And the final competence of the ministry headquarters is to perform other duties and tasks placed within its remit by this and other laws within the legal system of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the relevant period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bajagic, would you please comment on paragraph 162. And I would like to show you, in that respect, another document under tab 74 of P262.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, I've just managed to locate that under the tab number. But could you just remind me what paragraph you wanted me to comment on? Yes, I can see it now. Would you like me to comment on it? Well, paragraph 162, as we can see, it says that as a rule, pursuant to Article 33 on the Law on Internal Affairs that I commented on just a moment ago, the Law on Defence and the decision of the Presidency of the Serbian republic, MUP shall participate in the general mobilisation of conscripts. As I stressed earlier, the ambit of the ministry is not defined by the Law on Internal Affairs alone but also by other laws, and in that respect, I also mentioned that they also had a role in general mobilisation, which is in conjunction with Article 33, the last competence, as well as in keeping with the Law on Defence of June 1992. In other words, they are -- they have a role in the general public mobilisation of forces and resources in the republic in keeping with general legal provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now what we have under tab 74 is an order, as we can see, issued by the prime minister, pursuant to an order by the Presidency, or a decision adopted by the Presidency, as we can see in the preamble. And it also refers to the decision of the Presidency that you mention in your expertise. Now, would you please just comment briefly on paragraph 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 of this document, as we can see, describes that all military conscripts who do not comply with Article 1 of this decision, against all such military conscripts, measures shall be determined by the law and taken by the law. And then we see that in the second subparagraph, it says: "The implementation of these measures shall be pursued by members of the military police, the army and staff members of the Ministry of the Interior ..." In other words, this is directly related to paragraph 162 of my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, is this document, this order from the president of the government, in fact the implementation of the decision adopted by the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we can see, the first document that deals with this matter - in other words, mobilisation - came from the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the highest organ, and then we see that it is implemented by the government and the prime minister, and then it is further conveyed and assigned to lower levels, the ministries of internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now in paragraph 162, you also mention footnote 198. That's under tab 75. And it is marked here as 1422 in this particular case. Could you please take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 of the earlier document we just saw says that measures taken against individuals who do not comply with Article 1 on mobilisation, that the organisations in charge of taking such measures against these individuals are the army and Ministry of the Interior. Pursuant to the order from the government, we see that this is in keeping with Article 33 of the Law on Internal Affairs and that pursuant to that Article the ministry ordered -- issued an order to the special police unit to conduct mobilisation in certain municipalities -- or, rather, to mobilize those who have failed to report to call up, to a call-up up to a certain date and that all of this was in keeping with the decision by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina on general mobilisation. Now, under 2, paragraph 2 of this order, we see that all those conscripts who are mobilized pursuant to the decision there shall be handed over to the Lukavica Barracks, or referred to the Lukavica Barracks, and we see that, through the activity of one of its organisational units, they participated in the mobilisation process, and these individuals were handed over to the barracks, or, rather, a military post.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one question. Can you recognise the signature that appears on this document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it actually says that in the signature we see, it says that it's the minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic. However, we see there is some kind of symbol preceding the typed words "minister of the interior," and I assume that this would mean "for the minister of the interior" and that somebody else had actually placed their signature there. Because as far as I can recall, this does not look like the signature of the minister of the interior, because I believe I've seen that signature on one of the dispatches sent by -- on his behalf. So I believe this was signed on his behalf by someone at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, please tell me this. The ministry headquarters for the needs of the service, are they in a position to detach or resubordinate certain members of the internal affairs services and assign them to the territory of another municipality and not the one where they normally belong?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Internal Affairs is an organ that, by implication and also under the legal provisions, allows them to detach certain functional organisational units and also individuals, as we can see later on when we analyse the expertise, and assign them to certain tasks for a certain period of time in another territory and not the one where they normally belong. In other words, this could apply to a functional unit, such as the special police brigade, or it can apply to individuals, and individuals can be assigned to certain assignments outside of their own territory for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Bajagic. Now I would like you to give us your comments on paragraph 164 of your expert report. It deals with Article 38 of the Law on Internal Affairs, and perhaps it would be a good idea to put it back on our monitors. That's under tab 32; your footnote 142.3 of P530. Page [as interpreted] 38 is actually the fifth page of that document. And I believe it is the same in both versions, both in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please just repeat the tab number? I didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's 32.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your paragraph 164.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, if you need some assistance, perhaps we can ask the usher to remove one of the binders so that you can deal with them more easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Usher, if you can help Mr. Bajagic that just one of the binders is moved. Thank you very much, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 164 of my expert report, I analyse Articles -- I analyse the Article 38 of the Law on Internal Affairs because of something that that took me by surprise. This significantly, actually, restricts the role of the minister of the interior in the event of emergency situations, such as an imminent threat of war, and other emergencies, and I quoted parts of that Article which suggest that the minister could not issue any such orders without the approval of the assembly, such as, for instance, Assembly of Citizens in a specified public area. In other words, he was unable to issue such an order without the approval of the National Assembly or an order from the president if the National Assembly was unable to meet. And I refer there to a constitutional provision which provides for the president to issue certain orders in the event that the National Assembly is unable to do so at the time, which would then later just confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could we just briefly look at your paragraph 166. It deals with Article 40 of the law. And it is on the same page in Serbian, and I believe in English, it's on page 6.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can just say this briefly. We see the same phenomenon, in other words the restriction of the powers of the minister of the interior, in external communication. And Article 40 of the law specifies that it is only the president of the republic who can decide on which socio-political communities, the republic, town, municipality, or so forth are to be informed of the activities of the MUP. In other words, the minister did not have the power to inform other organs about the operations of the Ministry of the Interior without the approval of the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like you to comment on paragraph 175 of your expert report relating to Article 43 of the law, and I believe that's on the following page, page 6 in the B/C/S version, and we have the right page in English already. Again, that's paragraph 175 of your expert report.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 175 analyses Article 43 of the Law on Internal Affairs, which is of great significance in my view, because it regulates the question of who issues orders in the administrative procedure to authorised officials of the MUP, and I quoted there a sentence where it says: "Authorised officials must execute orders issued by the minister or by their immediate supervisor for the purpose of performing duties and tasks of national and public security except when such orders contravene the constitution and the law." The importance of this lies in the fact that it states that the Ministry of the Interior, as a state administration organ, uses the term "control and order," which indicates that orders and other instructions that the ministry headquarters send have the nature of an administrative document within that particular government agency. That was important for me, in order to be able to distinguish between this and the terms that are used in the military. That is why I say at the end of this paragraph that since the Law on State Administration and the Law on Ministries and the Law on the Ministry of the Interior define the ministry as a state administration organ. On that basis, I concluded -- and, anyway, it says in modern-day police science that as stated in paragraph 133 there is control within the police; whereas, in the military, there is command. So the way of issuing orders is quite different. That was important and that is why I quoted that. When I said that those who were issued orders to carry out tasks except those that contravene the constitution and the law. However, I think that we are going to explain that in detail at a different point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have a couple of issues in the transcript. I think quite some time ago, I think we seeked [sic] assistance from the CLSS in -- in relation to -- to the specific term "rukovodjenje," and I believe it was agreed that -- that the proper translation was "directing." Now I see here "control and order." But I think it was "directing," as opposed to "commanding." And there is one other thing. The administrative act, I -- I think needs to be explained by the -- by the expert because it has been translated as "administrative document." 43:5. But I will come to that. I will seek clarification from the expert. But about the -- the -- the "directing," I would like to -- to have it clear whether that -- that is the understanding of our friends from the Office of the Prosecutor, that it has been agreed like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I -- I -- I don't recall. If you can direct me to where there was a document or something we received from CLSS. I simply don't remember if it was something I dealt with before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I will provide the reference. We have to find it in the transcript. So we will return to that. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bajagic, when you say issuing orders in an administrative procedure as an act of administration, when they say that they have the nature of an administrative act, are you referring to a document, or what is it that you mean when you say that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean, or what I meant, is everything that leaves the Ministry of the Interior by way of internal documentation. That is, documents and specific documents, such as orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is the core of the matter the fact that administrative acts, both as acts and documents, are strictly prescribed by law or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, they are prescribed by law. We're going to see later in the analysis what kind of documents are issued by the ministry and which were relevant for this expert report as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does that make a distinction between the situation in administrative organs, in the one hand, and in the military, on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministry headquarters issues orders, how to act in general situations or in specific situations. Of course, this action has to be in line with the law. Members of the Ministry of the Interior, as authorised officials, I mean, by virtue of the fact that they received the status of authorised officials, they have the legal obligation to exercise certain authority, regardless of whether there are specific orders involved. I think that members of the ministry --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, I don't think you understand my question. What you say here and what you said in your answer a moment ago, you say in your paper that is why it says that the police --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is the difference involved.

utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... thank you very much. I did say direction in the police and commanding in the army, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a military system, the members of the military carry out their tasks on the basis of a direct order. In the police, it's different. On the basis of all regulations and administrative documents, the members of the police have certain powers to take action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please give us your comment on paragraph 178 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the administrative actions, or powers, is the right to ask persons to show their IDs and to bring them to an appropriate organ. That is defined by Article 47 of the Law on the Interior and authorised officials of the Ministry of the Interior --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have paragraph -- or, rather, Article 47 on our monitors, please. It's the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Ministry of the Interior can carry out this administrative action in accordance with this Article of the law and in ways envisaged by the law. utterances.text: Thank you.
