utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is the next page of the Serbian text. And I assume that it is the same in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 187, I provide my comment on the basis of Article 45 [as interpreted], one of the powers vested in the members of the Ministry of the Interior, that is to say, the right of authorised officials to collect data and information when this is necessary for the purpose of uncovering crimes and accomplices in the commission of these crimes. So this is one of the usual administrative actions taken by members of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serb Republic of BH and before that for the ministries and for all modern police forces anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I please have your comment on Article 55 of the law. And it is paragraph 189 of your expert report.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is an administrative action, or one of the powers that the members of the Ministry of the Interior have. It involves closing off access to a specific area or facility and preventing people from leaving the area or facility without permission. So, in my judgement, this administrative action, or, rather, this power of the members of the Ministry of the Interior, is, in most cases, envisaged in the field of uncovering crime and fighting crime as such. I provided a broader explanation here; but, in brief terms, I should say that without this kind of entitlement to this kind of administrative action, members of the crime prevention police could not efficiently secure the scene or take many other tactical measures from a crime-prevention point of view, in order to get to relevant facts that may be of assistance to uncover a crime and possibly obtain preliminary information for -- from persons who may be present there and thus collect information that may lead to uncovering the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that we have time to hear your comments on Article 56. It's the next page in Serbian. It is your paragraph 190.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 56 of the Law on Internal Affairs, as can be shown -- as can be seen from paragraph 190 of this expert report regulates the use of instruments of coercion, which is, as I have been pointing out, one of the standard administrative actions taken by all police forces in the world. According to this Article of the law, this right has been vested in the Ministry of the Interior; that is to say, its authorised officials. Also, this Article states what is meant by instruments of coercion. That is, physical force, rubber batons, police dogs, police cavalry, water hoses, gas weapons, and other gas devices, binding devices, devices for forcible obstruction and stopping of vehicles and individuals. So all this is specified, every one of these instruments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bajagic. Once again, I need to intervene in relation to the transcript. Last time when we discussed this with a previous witness we had a similar situation, and then Ms. Korner was so kind as to give us the right explanation or interpretation of this term "sredstvo prinude," how it should be translated. She said that in English in her view the best term to be used would be "use of force in the course of arrest," if I remember that correctly. I am going to find it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... That is my recollection, too, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. [Interpretation] For the purposes of the transcript, that's 19903. That's the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We still have time left to hear your comments in respect of paragraph 195.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which has to do with Article 159?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL'S LAST INTERVENTION WAS
utterances.text: "That is my recollection, too." I think it is important to add that in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, I'm sorry. I missed that Judge Hall was not recorded. Thank you. I know I'm creating a problem because I'm shifting. I sometimes speak in Serbian and then there is a translation going on and then ... but I'm ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will try my best to avoid making a confusion anymore. Thank you. [Interpretation] I apologise, I referred to Article 59. Yes, we have it before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the paragraph of your report we're dealing with is 195. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 195 of the expert report, I analysed Article 59 of the law, which is directly related to Articles 56 and 57 of the law. Article 59 regulates that the chief of the Security Services Centre shall, within the legal time-limit, that's to say, within seven days at the most, of being informed that an authorised official of one of the public security stations within the system of the centre, has used force in one of the ways described under Article 56, or fire-arm under Article 57, that he will have the duty to assess the legality and appropriateness of the use of force, one of the instruments thereof or fire-arm. In other words, the chief of the CSB shall have seven days to investigate this, to assess this, in respect of the use of force, or fire-arm, on the part of any of the officials of any of the SJBs the centre covers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, in view of the provisions of Article 59 and the inherent duty of a CSB chief, what is the obligation of the chiefs of SJBs in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stipulation of the law is that the chief of the CSB has the obligation to assess the lawfulness of the use of force within the prescribed time-limit, so whether it was used within the limits of the law and whether it was used properly. But the Article does not confer any duties or powers in this regard to any of the SJB chiefs. Rather, it is only the CSB chief who is referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I do agree with that. But as the law regulates, and you confirm in Article 59, the CSB chief is under the obligation to do this and that, within seven days of learning of this. So if a member of the Ministry of the Interior who is a member of any of the SJBs used force, including fire-arm, how is the SJB chief going to learn this?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he is definitely going to learn this or be informed of it from the chief of the SJB concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the clock. Perhaps this might be the right time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, if this is convenient. We return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bajagic, footnote 184 and 185 of your report, which relate to paragraphs 150 and 151, refer to the rule-book on the operation of public security. It's 889D1. Unfortunately, I don't have it in my binder. I asked for copies to be made, but until that time, we can look at it on our screens. Sir, these are 1977 rules of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Were these rules also applicable with regard to the duties performed by the Public Security Service of the MUP of Republika Srpska of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as was the case with some other bylaws regulating issues related to the workings of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska of Bosnia-Herzegovina, these rules were in force in 1992 as one of the documents which did not run contrary to the laws in force at the time in the Serbian Republic of BH. These rules, as well as others, were applied and adhered to by the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, these rules are on the affairs of public security. Do they contain detailed interpretations of all the relevant articles from the Law on Internal Affairs that we have discussed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1977 rules set out in detail the departments and structural units from the ministry headquarters down to the lowest territorial units, as well as the tasks and duties that the various units down to the level of departments and sections are duty-bound to carry out in keeping with these rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your view, is this document important for the understanding of the way in which the Ministry of the Interior operated when it comes to public security?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is certainly important. Some sections of the rules where the establishment of certain structural units is discussed, be it in territorial or hierarchical terms, also deal with the powers and competences these departments have to perform their tasks within the purview of the Ministry of the Interior. At any rate, together with the law and other bylaws the rules are very important in order to gain an insight into the workings of the Ministry of the Interior and its respective units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm told that the document is not in the law library due to apparently what was an oversight. On that basis, I'd like that the document be introduced into the law library or that it be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I thought that we had recently, when I say recently, since the Defence case opened, visited this question and the understanding was that the law library is not closed at this point. And as documents are newly discovered, then they would just be included. I don't know if the Prosecution has a different recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I don't. And I don't necessarily disagree with that. But I have a question and maybe it arises out of my confusion. But I thought we looked at the 1990 rules, earlier from January 29th on the rules on internal affairs. And if there's a 1990 version that is in effect in 1992, then I don't see a relevance of a 1977 version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a difference between two rule-books. utterances.text: Well, I believe I asked the question of the witness and he confirmed that this particular document from 1977 was in fact used in 1992 in the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bajagic, let's go back to paragraph 195 of your report and footnote 229, which is related to the paragraph. Was there rules governing the use of fire-arms?

That's tab 32, P530, your footnote 142.3. It's page 15 in Serbian and probably 16 in English. Article 127. Page 15. This has to do with paragraph 215.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 215, Article 127 is addressed, which stipulates the way in which all members of the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina are to be assumed by the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic. In other words, with the date of the coming into effect of this law, the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic would take on all of these members of the MUP, in accordance to their preferences. And it is stated in that Article that all employees in the headquarters and all the employees in the security stations on the respective posts that they held would be taken over by the Ministry of the Interior of Serbian Republic of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your view, on the basis of these legal provisions and in the course of your research, was it your conclusion that there existed certain restrictions or limitations with respect to those employees of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were of Serbian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Who were of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it says here that all other -- all employees of Serbian ethnicity and other ethnicities, that is to say, regardless of their ethnicity can voluntarily express a wish to be taken on by the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of BH. There were no restrictions. It was left up to them to say voluntarily whether they would move on to the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and continue their work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now show you the next document with a different subject. I will go back with you to paragraph 106 of your report and also paragraph 231, with which this document is also linked. And it has to do with footnote 131. That's Exhibit 1D159, tab 29.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please comment on this document for us, the one that you referred to in your footnote 131.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not opened it in my binder. Which tab is it? I'll do it very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's tab 29. And your paragraph in question is 106 and the related footnote, 131, in which you referred to this document.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As we mentioned yesterday, as I think, this has to do with the fact that deputy interior minister on 26th September 1992 issued an instruction on mobilising the reserve police force, which we connected with some other documents too. And considering the fact that such mobilisation could only be carried out on the basis of orders of federal organs, the organs of the federal state, as mentioned in the dispatch which we dealt with in connection with paragraph 107. So this was the manning and updating of the wartime organisation of the MUP which was signed by Deputy Minister Zepinic together with a form which is an integral part of the document and stating in which manner the information should be filled and updated. That was the information about the mobilisation of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can see that it says here the 26th of September 1992 in the record but I think you said and in your report it says 1991.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, 26th September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, as for the Ministry of the Interior of the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also other organs, were they obliged, according to the regulations that were in force in SFRY, to have defence plans and plans for extraordinary situations or emergencies.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly did. Not just state administration organs but also all enterprises, all educational and health institutions, considering the set of legal regulations which regulated specifically this issue, the situation of an imminent threat of war, war, and other emergency situations. It is certain that the constitution of SFRY which was then in force included several provisions that had to do with this subject, but systemic laws in this area, that is to say, the documents where the law on All People's Defence and the strategy of the All People's Defence and social self-protection. Of course, on the basis of the Law on All People's Defence and this strategy, in certain specific laws that primarily had to do with the Ministry of the Interior in that period, and it was called the secretariat of the interior, and also within the military system, the laws pertaining to them regulated this subject matter in accordance with the documents I already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would move to tender this document so it can be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, can I confirm which one we're talking about? Is this the Zepinic document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have a --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. It's already 1D159. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bajagic, before we move on to the actual situation, the organisation, and activities of MUP in 1992, I would ask you a few general questions relating to item 3 from paragraph 233 of your report and further. I believe that this is all connected. And in connection with this, I would show you a couple of documents. It is tab 6, 65 ter 444D1. I will ask you for your comment.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the tab number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document, or, rather, a decision which was made on the basis of item 2 of decision to form the Army of Republika Srpska, so this is the decision on the forming, organisation, establishment, and command and control of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was signed by the then-president of the presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Radovan Karadzic. So the decision is based on the decision to establish the Army of Republika Srpska and it deals with the organisation, forming of the Army of Republika Srpska, command and control, establishing the Main Staff, and generally speaking, which corps should make up the army, and where their seats would be and what would be the zones of responsibility of individual corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3 there is the signature of ... ?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President of the Presidency, Radovan Karadzic. I already emphasised that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, do you remember what was the assembly session at which the decision to establish the Army of Republika Srpska was made?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was made but I do not know the exact date. I know that the decision was made, that the documents referred to it, but I really could not guess the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would propose that we admit this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D534, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please comment on the next document. This is document number 7, 65 ter 500D1.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document deals with --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a second so that we can wait until we get the English text on the monitor so everyone could follow. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document or, rather, the order to form and establish the army of the Serbian Republic of BH is the result of the previous document that is to say, the decision made by the president of the Presidency. This order was issued and signed by the commander, Lieutenant-Colonel General Ratko Mladic, and on the basis of the previous document it talks about the seat of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and specifies in detail which units would belong to which corps of the Army of Republika Srpska. On principle, this document is a consequence of the decision to form and establish the Army of Republika Srpska which was signed by the president of the Presidency of Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic, and now this is specified by the chief of General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would move to have this document admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D535, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we are having a bit of a difficulty in accepting that these documents be admitted through this witness, who is an expert on police matters. Now, we realize that the documents are -- are, indeed, relevant, so we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it wasn't intended for -- for any specific comment by this witness because is he not expert on military issues. But I -- it is just to illustrate actually the -- the -- the time-line of the -- of the establishment of the -- of the -- of the military -- of the VRS at the time. It -- the problem is -- the problem is, Your Honours, that we came in possession of these documents only after the -- the Office of the Prosecutor military expert has stepped down. Otherwise, I would have, of course, shown it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My point, I think, perhaps was not clear. My point is that we should limit ourselves to introducing documents into evidence through particular witnesses who are capable of testifying to them, and since this witness is a professor and expert on police and MUP matters, it may not appear to be quite appropriate to have documents relating to something completely different introduced through this witness. You may have other witnesses through whom it would be more appropriate to -- to introduce these documents. But let's not dwell too long on this. I'm just giving you a signal that this is on the border-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand and I appreciate it. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I initially started to rise, Your Honour, because I was going to complain that this is something that should have been shown to Ewan Brown when he testified here. But I understand that Mr. Zecevic says that he didn't get the document until after Mr. Brown testified. However, I think your point is a good one. And I see that Mr. Zupljanin has a military expert on his list as a witness to be called later in this case, and perhaps would be a more appropriate witness to deal with this document, in which case, I would suggest that we have this one MFI'd at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For tidiness, I suppose, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Therefore, Your Honours, Exhibits 1D534 and 1D535 will remained marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bajagic, as we have dealt with the de jure aspect of your research, we have arrived to the de facto part. That's primarily paragraph 219 and onwards. Would you be so kind to provide us with a general comment on paragraph 219 and generally what you discuss in this part of your report.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the analysis of the factual situation concerning the organisation and functioning of the MUP in the course of the year 1992, I started by noting in paragraph 219 that, considering the de jure situation, that is to say the obligation of the Ministry of the Interior to act in accordance with the specific law and other documents which we mentioned, that the status of the ministry, its organisation, and its functioning, according strictly to organisations, was considerably limited by the actual situation on the ground. In particular, it was a problem to establish, strictly legally speaking, the organisational structure, the management and control, and everything else that the ministry is supposed to do, because some significant documents such as the constitution and constitutional law, the constitution of the Serbian Republic of BH is what I mean, the constitutional law on the implementation of the constitution, limited some sections of the Law on the Internal Affairs, and, therefore, prevented the Ministry of the Interior to act fully in accordance with the law. That is on the one hand. On the other, as we know, there was a number of Serbian autonomous regions, as well as the Autonomous Region of Krajina. These were the regional organisational units in the area of the Serbian Republic of BH, and as late as September 1992, they began to be gradually incorporated in accordance with the amendments which were used to change certain constitutional provisions, and they were gradually being incorporated within the legal system of the Serbian Republic of BH, which late on became Republika Srpska. So there were the two facts which were limiting this: The constitution and constitutional law; the fact that there was the Autonomous Region of Krajina and Serbian autonomous regions on the ground which only in 1992, after the adoption of constitutional amendments, began to be gradually incorporated into a single and unified system of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to what you've just said to us, could you give us a brief comment on paragraph 222.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, before we come to that question for the witness, first, could you clarify, explain, what you mean by: The ministry was prevented to act fully in accordance with the law and that, on the basis of constitution. How am I to understand this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, from 1992, and the constitutional law, recognised the existence of autonomous regions as regional, territorial entities, and Serb autonomous regions. They recognised them in the sense of recognising that in that territory they have certain legal regulations regulating the life and work of those regions. The Ministry of the Interior -- or, rather, the Law on the Ministry of the Interior does not in its text recognise any other subject matter except for that which is related to the functioning of the Ministry of the Interior. So, when we look at the factual situation, the ministry worked in increasingly difficult conditions because it could not function within a single territory. It was not a unified, single territory, and that became possible only through the constitutional amendments. When the Serb autonomous regions were no longer recognised but only this single line of functioning from the central government towards the local lower level -- levels of government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, the ministry could not function in the autonomous regions on the same level as in the other parts of the republic. Is that basically what you're trying to explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you can put it that way. That it could not fully carry through what running all the organisations of the MUP in the territory meant. Some organisational units, especially CSBs, were within the system of this -- of this system of autonomous regions or Serb autonomous regions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bajagic, are you trying to suggest, or is it your conclusion, that in terms of this aspect, there is some division into two periods during 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many paragraphs of this expert report reflect that. I think we can speak about two periods. One up until September, functioning under increasingly difficult conditions, in terms of running all the organisational units involved; and then, after September 1992. Although we can say that establishing this unified territory and this unified way of running the organisational units, that did not happen all of a sudden. It happened over the course of a few months, so we can say that only towards the end of 1992 this has been set in place -- or, rather, the Ministry of the Interior was established in accordance with the Law on the Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65:25, the minister said in accordance with -- oh, sorry, not the minister. The witness. In accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs the way it was envisaged by the Law on Internal Affairs. That's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In accordance with what was envisaged by the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, to complete the picture, I'll take you back to paragraphs 145, 146, and 147 of your expert report. At one point in time today, you started speaking about that, and I interrupted you - I apologise for that - but I said that we will be getting to that, and now is the time for that. Can you please explain? It has to do with Article 27 of the law. We're going back to the law. That is tab 32. P530, Article 27. Could you explain what this pertains to.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this set of paragraphs, when analysing Article 27 of the Law on Internal Affairs, it is stated that organisational units of the Ministry of the Interior, in addition to the tasks specified in the regulations, are -- they are duty-bound to carry out regulations passed by the municipal assemblies relating to public law and order and road traffic safety, as well as other regulations passed by the municipal assemblies. I particularly pointed out the fact that the rules on the internal organisation of the ministry of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was involved in a procedure only from the Autumn onwards, so it was the rules that were from 1990. The rules on internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1990. So organisational units, like the CSBs -- the SJBs, rather, had certain obligations vis-a-vis the local governments in peacetime and in a state of imminent threat of war. And these obligations of theirs were based on the already mentioned Law on National Defence of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, when you say here -- or, rather, when Article 27 of the law says that public security stations have the obligation of implementing regulations passed by the municipal assembly relating to law and order and road safety, as well as other regulations in the domain of internal affairs, can you give us an example of what kind of regulations this pertains to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, these can be some situations that are specific in terms of a particular municipality. For example, in the territory of a particular municipality, there can be something that is special in relation to others. For example, a sports hall where events of national and international significance may be taking place, and then such institutions can follow the situation together with the Secretariat of Interior, with the SJB. They can provide safety and security so that this kind of major events could be held in the first place. These are situations that are of relevance to all citizens in the territory of a municipality, or, rather, within a local self-government. At any rate, everything that has to do with public law and order and, generally speaking, as far as public law and order is concerned, in a society by definition it is not only the police or the Ministry of the Interior that is the only institution involved. It is the society at large that has to be involved as well, and that is why there has to be this kind of cooperation between organs of local government and public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. That is what I wanted to ask you about. I would like you to comment on paragraph 147 of your expert report and Article 32 of the law. And that paragraph of yours pertains to that particular Article. I would just like you to provide us with a brief comment, and I believe that that would be it for the day, because I think that we have to adjourn early.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my comment with regard to paragraph 147 is just a continuation of the previous comment, in view of the provisions of the law referred to. Assemblies and the executive organs of local government may send certain proposals to the ministry headquarters, as well as opinions and initiatives that are related to matters that are of relevance to the overall safety and security of the municipality, and in that connection, the work of centres of public security and public security stations. As the law says, the ministry is duty-bound to look at initiatives, opinions, and proposals, and inform the organs of local government in a municipality of their own views regarding these initiatives or certain measures that may have been taken in relation to such initiatives. So according to this law, the MUP was duty-bound to consider these initiatives and to respond within a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: From the point of view of this comment of yours, I'm just giving an example by way of illustration. For instance, if the municipality of Visegrad were to launch an initiative to close down a road across the old bridge on the Drina, and that is something that is related to traffic safety, would that be an illustration of the kind of situation that you have been telling us about now?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course. That could be an illustration of that kind. Perhaps, since this is a historical monument in this specific case, that would be it precisely, to restrict traffic along certain roads, in order to improve traffic safety or public law and order. Or there can be a different situation. For example, a marathon or another race, and, of course, a town could ask for the police to take active part in this, not only from the point of view of their regular work. Rather, they should make an extra effort in order to ensure the success of such an event.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honours, I see Ms. Korner has arrived and this is about the proper place for me to stop for the day and continue tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, we are about to take the adjournment for the day, but we have certain procedural matters with which to deal before the Court rises. So the usher will escort you from the courtroom at this point. Tomorrow, we are scheduled to resume in the afternoon and in a different courtroom. But you will be conducted to the appropriate place at the appropriate time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we hear from Ms. Korner, who we understand has requested the time to deal with certain matters there are two matters which the Chamber -- to which the Chamber wishes to speak. Firstly, upon the Registry's request, the Chamber clarifies that its order of the 20th of April, 2011, whereby it rescinded the protective measures of ST-219 also applies to the audio and video record of his testimony in this case on the 22nd of November, 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Brother. The second issue we have is just to put a question to Mr. Krgovic, because we noted that you filed a motion, I think it was on the 15th of April, for protective measures for your witnesses. And it states, at least in the English translation, that you wish to have this motion cover all the viva voce witnesses that you intend to call; yet, towards the end of that same motion, you only address protective measures for three witnesses. I understand, and I recall, that you have asked for, all together, 13 viva voce witnesses. So my question to you, Mr. Krgovic, are you seeking protective measures for all 13 witnesses that you call viva voce or only those three that you have mentioned in your motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this must be due to an error when the submission was filed. I thought that I clearly stated in my motion that we sought protective measures only in respect of the three witnesses that were specifically named in that motion. The other witnesses will be testifying viva voce in open session without any protective measures. That's the situation for the time being. We haven't received any information from our investigators on the field of any other witnesses appearing viva voce and seeking protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification, Mr. Krgovic. You may wish to consult paragraph 2 of your motion to see if there's a mistake in the translation. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm really sorry to trouble Your Honours with what really is an administrative matter, the first thing I wish to raise. Your Honours will recall that on the Thursday before Easter, Maundy Thursday, I spent a little time asking Mr. Bjelosevic about documents and asking him if he was agreeable to produce various documents for us, which he was, and the question then arose as to the best way of doing it. And it was decided that VWS should be the people to deal with it. And at page 19977, I asked him this at line 22: "Are you prepared to have someone from the Sarajevo field office to collect these documents in advance," and I under line this, "because otherwise it will mean a delay when you get here while we all look at the documents." And as I say it was then changed to VWS. Regrettably my understanding is that as follows that between Maundy Thursday when he left, and yesterday, there was no contact between him and VWS at all. VWS turned up yesterday and delivered to him, and I don't know why, the bundle of documents that he had had here which we all understood he was going to take back with him simply to identify which documents he had provided and which the CSB Doboj. He never had that bundle throughout the whole ten-day period and VWS turned up yesterday and just gave it to him. They did not ask him if he discovered any other documents, as I understand it. The arrangement now is that he will give them any documents he can find on the 9th which is next Monday, which is much too late, because if he doesn't give them to VWS in Sarajevo until the 9th, we are unlikely to get them here before I would imagine however they're going to bring them up on the Thursday and he is due to come back on the Monday. And if any of the documents are to be translated or looked at by us, that really does not give very much time. Accordingly, I have asked if VWS could contact him -- I asked if they could contact him yesterday. I understand their position is they will not do so unless this is a direction from the Trial Chamber. I would be very grateful, therefore, if Your Honours would district VWS to contact him and ask him if he can produce those documents by the latest Thursday of this week, as it is now Tuesday, to them, so that, with luck, we could have them by the 9th. And I understand -- I spoke to Mr. Zecevic about this, to whom it most affects and he's in agreement with the course that we suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, have you something to add, Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 15 seconds. I have an administrative obligation towards the Registry to report my presence here today. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So with the assistance of the Court Officer we give the necessary direction. I'm saying that for the record but to the extent that the Registry may need further clarification, we will take the liberty of doing that out of court, for the benefit of the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm perfectly content with that. I understand that they just needed an order from Your Honours, a direction. The second matter is even more administrative. It relates to a document that was marked 2D89, MFI. Your Honours may recall, it's a payroll list from Doboj. It was put in by Mr. Krgovic during originally on the 31st of May? I think, 31st of May. And indeed at that stage the OTP was saying that there ought to be a translation of the writing that -- the handwriting that appeared on the document before it was admitted. So it was MFI'd. Mr. Krgovic put it again in cross-examination to Mr. Bjelosevic, and at that stage the same problem over the untranslated words at the top came up. We sent it off for a revised translation which we got, and we asked the Defence, please, we sent it to the Defence, to upload it into e-court and they declined to do that. I have no doubt that Mr. Krgovic will explain why. But, Your Honour, all that we're asking at the moment, leaving aside whether it becomes a full exhibit or not, is if the Defence decline to upload the revised translation into e-court, we ask that the document be released and we will upload the revised translation. It was originally a document provided by us. We can then argue about whether it becomes an exhibit later. But, at the movement, I say, because the Defence won't upload it, we would like to do that. So could we have the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I provide an explanation for this. The document was disclosed to us for the first time during the testimony of a witness from Doboj, a chief of -- or, rather, the chief of the public security station in Doboj. The Prosecution didn't use it at the time but I did use with Witness Radulovic. I asked that the document be admitted into evidence. However, if you look at transcript pages 1107 to 1111, the Prosecution opposed the admission on the grounds of the fact that it was a poor copy. And then, later on, when we were settling the matter of all the documents that were tendered, we placed them all on the list, but the Prosecution yet again opposed their admission at the end of their case. In the meantime, we produced our own draft translation, because we believed that the document was translatable. We sent the draft translation to the translation service, which rejected our request, stating that they were unable to translate the document. Now, once all these witnesses testified, and once the Prosecution case is over, the translation service is providing us with a better translation than was the one that we produced. The translation we provided was a fair one, and yet the translation service rejected the request for a final translation. So this is a -- an important issue to us and I want the CLSS to state the reasons why they rejected our request for the translation of this document, whilst they actually accepted the request from the Prosecution and translated the document. I am interested in the specifically names, date and the stamp on this document, and this is what we don't have on the translation version we have now, and on that ground, we oppose its admission. And let me state that the CLSS version and the Prosecution differ in only slight details.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Well, I understand that Mr. Krgovic is aggrieved by the fact that CLSS acted on our request but wouldn't have his. But that's not the point. The point at the moment now is that there is a revised translation. It does show the handwritten name and therefore there's no reason at all why it should not be uploaded into e-court. As I said, the argument about whether the document becomes a full exhibit is a separate matter. All we want at the moment is for the revised translation to be uploaded into e-court. Otherwise we can't show it to Your Honours when we have the discussion and the Defence won't do it. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may just shortly observe. It is my understanding that the translation which was provided by the CLSS on request of the Office of the Prosecutor, again, is not the full translation. That is the problem. And Mr. Krgovic is having a problem because this, again, is a partial translation. So I suggest that the Trial Chamber instructs the CLSS to do their utmost to translate the whole document and give us the whole document and then we will admit it. I think the both parties basically agree [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ... that's precisely the point. The CLSS should take into consideration the draft translation we sent to them originally. I agree fully with what Mr. Zecevic said. We need a complete translation. We tried to assist the CLSS back in June by enlarging the copy, by providing them with our own translation, and yet they rejected our request. What we need is a full translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... All right, Your Honours. I don't want to waste any more of Your Honours' time on this. Perhaps Your Honours would direct, please, CLSS, using whatever assistance they can get from the Defence, to produce the fullest possible translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So directed. Whatever assistance we can afford. And with that, we can take the adjournment -- there was something else? No. So with that, we take the adjournment to tomorrow at 2.15. Courtroom III, I believe.
